title: In search of the "Make it fast with AI" button
author: Fishpedition
selftext:
I'm developing a browser game about a scientific expedition to Lake Tanganyika in 1896. You dive underwater, catch real and hybrid fish, describe species, and sell your finds.

Everything runs on a server: 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, PostgreSQL, Node.js, Redis, RabbitMQ. All in Docker.

I write a significant portion of the code with an AI agent. I spent two entire days of my weekend working on just one task, performance optimization:

1. **Find what's actually eating up server resources**

I was convinced Node.js was the bottleneck, but it turned out I was wrong. Under load, Node.js was using about 75% of a single core. PostgreSQL was using almost 2 out of 4 cores.

More than half of the database's processing time was spent on one small UI element, an "Almost There" hint. For example, "You only need to catch 3 more fish to overtake another player in the rankings."

This block ran on every expedition results screen: 8 ms × 581,000 calls.

2. **Fix the problem and measure again**

After optimization, query execution time dropped from 16 ms to 1.6 ms with 3,000 players.

Before and after optimization under load:

* Requests per second: 280 → 303
* Expedition page: 83 ms → \~40 ms (median)
* Database CPU usage: 182% → 157%, while the server handles more requests

3. **Find the limit and test it yourself**

After this optimization, under load from concurrently running bots, throughput stopped increasing while latency continued to grow.

The current limit is around 20 expeditions per second. If a real player completes one expedition every few minutes, that's \~3,500 people online on a single server.

While the server was running at its limit, I logged into the game myself and started playing. I tested quick dives near the shore, long trips, and maximum depth.

I didn't notice any lag.

My main takeaway from this weekend. Figuring out what actually needs to be fixed is still up to you. You need to measure, analyze the numbers, and recognize when your own assumptions turn out to be wrong.

I know what I'll be doing next weekend. But if you've found the "Make it fast with AI" button, let me know.
